description: We’re the Apogeans, a team from Muscat hooked on one question: where on Earth can we practise living on the Moon and Mars? We’re using NASA data to match future base sites with real places here, like deserts, craters and ice fields, even Oman’s own Dhofar desert. Apogee is the highest point of an orbit, and that’s where we’re aiming. Other worlds. Found here.
summary:
We made Elsewhere, a free app that helps you find places on Earth that are similar to the Moon and Mars.

Astronauts and rover teams practise on Earth before going to space. They use deserts, volcanoes and cold, dry places that feel like the Moon or Mars. But only a few well-known sites are used, and there is no easy way to compare places.

With Elsewhere, you pick any country and the app shows the places there that are most like real Moon and Mars sites, such as the Artemis landing areas. Each place gets a score out of 100%. The app also shows why: what is similar, what is different, and the NASA data used. You can check any location, scan the whole Moon or Mars, or use your camera to see how Mars-like a landscape looks. It works offline on Android phones.

This matters because better practice sites help prepare better missions. It also lets every country find its own analog sites, not just a few. In Oman, for example, the app found that the Hajar Mountains are a good match for a canyon on Mars. We want students and researchers anywhere to be able to explore space from their own country.
details:
Elsewhere helps you find places on Earth that are like the Moon and Mars. You pick a country and the app shows the places there that best match 30 real Moon and Mars sites, such as Artemis landing areas, past landing spots and possible future bases. Each place gets a score out of 100%.

To make this work, we describe every place with the same 16 features, like how dry, cold, rocky or rugged it is, whether it has volcanic rock, red soil, salt, dunes or ice. We do this for Earth, the Moon and Mars, then compare the features to get a similarity score. The app also shows why a place matched, what is different, and which data was used. You can check any location, scan the whole Moon or Mars, rate a photo or use your camera, play trivia, and see a live space clock.

Benefits

  • It works for every country, not just a few famous sites.
  • Each result is explained, so people can trust it and learn from it.
  • It works offline, with no account and no personal data stored. Photos stay on the phone.
  • It runs on ordinary Android phones and in any web browser.

Intended impact

We want to help space agencies and researchers find better places to train and test before going to the Moon and Mars. We also want students and teachers everywhere to discover that their own country has places like the Moon or Mars, and to feel part of space exploration. In Oman, for example, the app found the Hajar Mountains are a strong match for a canyon on Mars.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python
  • Libraries: D3.js and TopoJSON for maps
  • Android: an Android WebView app, built with apktool
  • Data: NASA SRTM, MODIS and NASA POWER for Earth; LOLA, Diviner and LROC for the Moon; MOLA and THEMIS for Mars; plus WorldClim, ESA WorldCover and USGS geologic maps
  • Films: three.js, Playwright and FFmpeg
  • AI: Claude helped us analyze the large amount of data and write parts of the code
  • Hardware: our laptops and Android phones for testing

How it is creative

Instead of a scientific report, we turned a hard question into a simple score anyone can understand. We added fun ways to explore, like pointing your camera at a landscape to see how Martian it looks, trivia built from our own data, and a guided demo mode. We also made short cinematic films to tell the story.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: the data is global and fairly coarse, so we show scores as estimates and always show the data behind them.
  • Access: offline use, low-end phones and no sign-in, so people in remote areas can use it.
  • Privacy: no personal data is collected.
  • Fairness: every country gets the same treatment.
  • Clarity: simple words and clear explanations.
  • Space Apps rules: no NASA logos, AI-generated content labelled, and everything in English
